paper_title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Embodied foundation models, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models, connect visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, offering path toward general-purpose robot control (Black et al., 2024; Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024). Their generalization depends on diverse interaction experience across tasks, objects, and environments, yet collecting such data through robot teleoperation remains costly. Egocentric human videos provide complementary source of experience, capturing everyday manipulation without requiring robot hardware or teleoperation (Grauman et al., 2022; Hoque et al., 2026; Punamiya et al., 2026). Using this experience for policy learning, however, requires bridging the human-to-robot embodiment gap: the same operation can involve different motions and control mechanisms across humans and robots, and is often performed in scenes that differ from the robots workspace. 1 Figure 1 Overview of SALA. Left: unpaired human and robot videos are related only through language descriptions of their atomic actions. Middle: supervising latent action tokenizer with these relations organizes latent actions by action semantics rather than by scene. Right: through the aligned latent actions, human videos supervise the same policy that controls the robot: more human-video pre-training lowers the validation error of robot action prediction without additional robot data, and more task-specific human video in post-training raises the real-world success rate. Latent action models (LAMs) are popular way to incorporate human videos into robot policy training without explicit action labels (Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024b; Bu et al., 2025). By encoding visual transitions in shared latent space, they provide common prediction target for human and robot experience. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), which predict future video frames together with actions (Wu et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026b), LAMs avoid explicit pixel prediction during policy learning, which can make training more efficient. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which constrains each latent to explain the transition within its own clip but does not relate human and robot executions of the same behavior. Their latents therefore tend to cluster by visual appearance, such as the scene, rather than by the underlying action, so semantically similar human and robot actions need not lie close together. Aligning human actions with their robot counterparts thus requires supervision that connects their meanings across embodiments. Our insight is that language can provide this supervision. Even when human and robot clips are unpaired, natural-language descriptions of their atomic actions, such as grasp the cup, relate human clip to multiple robot clips with different degrees of semantic similarity, as illustrated on the left of figure 1. We propose SALA, which trains latent action tokenizer by translating these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents. Robot latents, grounded in control by action reconstruction, serve as anchors, and the alignment moves only human latents toward them. As the middle of figure 1 shows, the resulting latent actions are organized by action semantics rather than by scene, giving human videos prediction target that is meaningful for robot control. Once trained, the tokenizer labels videos from their frames alone, so its latent actions provide unified supervision signal for training the policy on both human and robot videos, without action labels or atomicaction descriptions. This makes human video scalable source of supervision along two axes. In pre-training, the policy can absorb large-scale general human videos spanning diverse everyday tasks. In post-training, the policy can further learn from task-specific human videos, i.e., videos of humans performing the target task. Because their latent actions are aligned with those of the robot, what the policy learns from these videos transfers directly to robot control. Since recording such videos requires neither robot nor teleoperation, they offer cheap way to improve the policy on new task beyond what fixed budget of teleoperated demonstrations provides. We evaluate SALA in simulation and on real robot. On RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025b), where videos of another robot arm stand in for human videos, SALA achieves higher average success rate than existing LAMs and WAMs trained on the same data. Analyses of the tokenizer show that language alignment organizes latent actions by atomic action semantics rather than by scene. On real robot controlled in 63DoF action space, including two 22-DoF dexterous hands, human video helps along both axes. Pre-training 2 on more general human video, up to 2,678 hours, consistently reduces the robots action prediction error on downstream tasks without additional robot data. With teleoperated demonstrations fixed, post-training on more task-specific human video raises the average real-robot success rate from 53.75% to 72.5%. The right of figure 1 shows both trends. Our contributions are as follows: We use language as relational supervision: atomic-action descriptions align human and robot latent actions from unpaired videos, with the alignment anchored on robot latents grounded in control. Through the aligned latent actions, we supervise the robot policy with both general human videos and human demonstrations of the target task. Experiments in simulation and on 63-DoF real robot show that SALA outperforms prior LAMs and WAMs trained on the same data, and that both uses of human video scale: more general human video keeps lowering the validation error of robot action prediction, and more task-specific human video raises real-world success rates.

sections.title: 2 Method
sections.content: Our goal is to use action-free egocentric human videos, which can be collected at scale, to facilitate the training of robot policies. We connect these videos to robot control through latent actions. This connection requires latent actions to establish semantic correspondence across embodiments, which shared latent space trained only by reconstructing each clip does not guarantee. As outlined in figure 2, SALA therefore learns latent action tokenizer aligned across embodiments by language supervision from atomic-action descriptions, and uses it to leverage human videos in robot policy training.

sections.title: 2.1 Preliminaries: Latent Action Models
sections.content: LAMs learn compact representations of visual transitions without action labels by coupling inverse and forward dynamics (Zhang et al., 2025a). Given observations ot and ot+k separated by horizon k, an inverse-dynamics encoder infers latent action = Eθ(ot, ot+k) that encodes the transition between the two observations. An information bottleneck produces (cid:101)z = Qϕ(z), limiting how much information from the future observation reaches the decoder. The forward-dynamics decoder Gv then reconstructs ot+k from the current observation ot and the compressed code (cid:101)z. Training minimizes the reconstruction error in image or feature space over observed pairs (Ye et al., 2025; Oquab et al., 2024; Kingma and Welling, 2013). The inferred codes can serve as prediction targets for policy learning from action-free videos (Ye et al., 2025; Bu et al., 2025). Their usefulness, however, depends on what they encode: accurate reconstruction does not guarantee that the latent captures controllable actions, since it may also retain scene information or changes unrelated to control (Zhang et al., 2025a). For human-to-robot transfer, the representation must additionally connect semantically related behaviors across embodiments, relation that reconstruction within individual clips does not explicitly constrain. We therefore augment this predictive formulation with robot action supervision and language-guided cross-embodiment alignment.

sections.title: 2.3 Robot-Anchored Semantic Transfer
sections.content: We align human latent actions toward the robot representations grounded by action reconstruction in section 2.2. These robot representations serve as control anchors, while atomic-action descriptions determine how each human clip should relate to them. Atomic-action descriptions characterize what clip does independently of the embodiment performing it. We therefore encode ℓ with frozen text encoder and use the similarity between language descriptions to measure how semantically related human clip is to each robot clip. Because human and robot clips are collected independently, human clip rarely has an exact robot counterpart. It can nonetheless relate to several robot clips to different degrees; for example, grasping cup is closer to grasping bottle than to placing cup. We therefore describe each human clip by soft neighborhood over the robot clips in batch, given by softmax over its language similarities, and use it to supervise the clips neighborhood in latent space. sections.title: 2.4 Latent-Action-Supervised Policy Learning
sections.content: After training, the tokenizer is frozen and serves as teacher that labels human and robot clips with latent actions. For clip (ot, ot+k), the teacher outputs its latent action tokens y, each categorical distribution over the codebook. We keep these distributions rather than discretizing them into code indices, retaining the graded similarity structure of the latent space. The future observation ot+k is used only to compute y; the policy itself observes only the current observation, so neither the teacher nor future frames are needed at deployment. As shown in figure 2(b), our policy adopts π0-style architecture (Black et al., 2024): vision-language model (VLM) encodes observations and language, and an action expert generates action chunks by flow matching. We add learnable latent-action queries to the action expert, which predict the token distributions ˆy through latent head, and let the noisy action tokens attend to these queries, so that latent-action prediction directly conditions action generation. For human videos, which provide neither states nor actions, the action expert processes only the latent queries. sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: Our experiments test the central claim of SALA: language-aligned latent actions turn videos of other embodiments into supervision for robot policies that is both effective and scalable. After summarizing the implementation in section 3.1, we evaluate the two properties in turn. For effectiveness, section 3.2 compares SALA on standardized simulation benchmark with existing LAMs and WAMs trained on the same cross-embodiment data. For scalability, section 3.3 asks whether SALA keeps improving the target robot in the real world as more human video is used, both with increasing human-video pre-training budgets and in task-specific post-training. We then ablate the design choices of our tokenizer and analyze whether its latent actions are aligned across embodiments in section 3.4. 3.

sections.title: Implementation Details
sections.content: We summarize the main configuration here. The tokenizer encodes each clip, whose two observations are separated by dataset-specific horizon k, into 8 latent tokens, quantized by SoftVQ with codebook of 256 codes; visual reconstruction targets frozen DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) features of the future observation, and atomic-action descriptions are embedded by frozen text encoder, CLIP ViT-B/32 in simulation and Qwen3-Embedding-4B (Zhang et al., 2025b) in the real world. The policy uses Qwen3-VL-4B (Bai et al., 2025) as the VLM and separately parameterized Qwen3-style transformer with 0.6B parameters as the action expert, which attends jointly with the VLM at every layer. The VLM is initialized from the pretrained Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct weights and the action expert from scratch, and each subsequent training stage starts from the checkpoint of the previous one. Experiment-specific tokenizer settings, loss weights, and further architectural details are given in section C.

sections.title: 3.3 Scalability in the Real World

We examine two levels: scaling human-video pre-training to 2,678 hours, and scaling human demonstrations of each downstream task in post-training. Setup. All real-world experiments are conducted on Sharpa North wheeled humanoid equipped with two 22-DoF Sharpa Wave dexterous hands, whose 63-dimensional joint-space action covers the arms, hands, torso, and neck; section details the platform. As summarized in table 1, we use action-free egocentric human videos DH for 2,678 equivalent hours of pre-training, alongside 888 hours of robot teleoperation data DR. sections.title: 4 Related Work
sections.content: Vision-language-action models. VLA models build on pre-trained vision-language models to map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026a). Their generalization depends on the diversity of robot data, which is costly to collect through teleoperation. Language has also been used to structure action learning in VLAs, through interpretable action primitives (Weng et al., 2026) or language-conditioned action priors learned without visual input (Lin et al., 2026). SALA keeps the VLA design, with flow-matching action expert, and adds latent-action prediction so that videos without action labels can supervise the same action expert. Learning from human videos. Human videos have been used to pre-train visual representations for robot manipulation (Nair et al., 2022). Closer to policy learning, one line of work extracts explicit motion from human videos, such as hand trajectories or poses, and maps it to robot actions (Wang et al., 2023; Kareer et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025); this requires hand tracking 11 and correspondence between human and robot kinematics. With sufficiently diverse pre-training, co-training VLAs on such human data can yield human-to-robot transfer (Kareer et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026). Another line predicts future observations as proxy for actions: generating video plans that are then converted into actions (Du et al., 2023; Ko et al., 2023), predicting subgoal images (Zhao et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026), or training WAMs that predict videos jointly with actions (Wu et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026b; NVIDIA et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Other work predicts future representations rather than pixels (Su et al., 2026; Miao et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026); when co-training on egocentric human videos, feature and 3D-flow targets transfer to robots better than pixel targets (Li et al., 2026a). Video prediction requires modeling scene appearance in addition to motion, and in section 3.2 some WAMs degrade sharply under domain randomization. SALA instead supervises the policy with latent actions, which require neither hand tracking nor pixel-level prediction. Instead of labeling videos with an inverse dynamics model trained on action-labeled Latent action models. data (Baker et al., 2022), latent action models infer actions from consecutive frames without action labels, by learning latents that predict the next frame (Schmidt and Jiang, 2023; Bruce et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Liang et al., 2026). They have been used to pre-train policies on actionless videos, including human videos (Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024b; Bu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026c). Because the latents are learned by reconstructing each clip, they can capture scene changes and distractors rather than the action (Zhang et al., 2025a). Prior work addresses this by conditioning on task instructions (Bu et al., 2025), by structuring the latent space (Li et al., 2026c), by contrastive disentanglement with action-category priors (Dai et al., 2026), or by adversarially suppressing embodimentand environment-specific factors (Liu et al., 2026). To relate embodiments, other methods align latents with robot actions recorded alongside the videos (Zhang et al., 2026a; Fan et al., 2026), with action labels of human hands (Luo et al., 2026), through paired human-robot demonstrations (Zhu et al., 2026), or through the shared visual consequences of heterogeneous kinematics (Chen et al., 2026a); related approach contrastively aligns the action spaces of human hands, dexterous hands, and grippers (Bauer et al., 2026). SALA instead uses atomic-action descriptions to relate unpaired human and robot clips by graded semantic similarity, and aligns human latents to robot latents grounded in control, so that human and robot executions of semantically similar actions receive similar latents.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented SALA, which uses language to align human and robot latent actions for policy learning. Naturallanguage descriptions of atomic actions relate unpaired human and robot clips through graded semantic similarity, and SALA turns these relations into soft neighborhood targets that move human latents toward robot latents grounded in control. The resulting latent actions let both general human videos and human demonstrations of the target task supervise the same policy that controls the robot. Experiments show that this supervision is scalable and effective. Our study has limitations that point to future work. The tokenizer requires atomic-action descriptions for its training clips, although the policy itself learns from video frames alone. Our pre-training scaling analysis covers up to 2,678 hours; whether the trend holds at larger scales remains open.

sections.content: A Cross-Embodiment Retrieval Protocol. As in section 3.4, each query clip of non-target embodiment retrieves the most similar targetrobot clip over all tasks, using the similarity of the alignment loss, i.e., the cosine similarity between prequantization latents averaged over tokens. Besides the reconstruction-only tokenizer and SALA, we report two references: Random, uniformly sampled robot clip, and Language, which retrieves by the similarity of atomic-action descriptions. On RoboTwin 2.0, ARX-X5 clips from 47 tasks query all Aloha-AgileX clips; we check whether the retrieved clip performs the same atomic action and measure the distance between the end-effector displacements of the two clips. In the real world, human clips query all robot teleoperation clips. For queries from the 56 tasks shared with the robot data, we check whether the retrieved clip comes from the same task and whether both hands perform the same verbs. For these queries and for those from tasks absent from the robot data, we also compute the similarity between the atomic-action descriptions of the query and the retrieved clip, rescaled so that Random scores 0 and Language scores 1. Alignment improves every metric in table 6. On RoboTwin 2.0, the two embodiments share the viewpoint and workspace, so reconstruction alone already retrieves the same atomic action for 41.3% of queries; alignment raises this to 78.2%, with gains in all 47 tasks. In the real world, human and robot videos differ in viewpoint, embodiment, and background, and reconstruction alone is close to random. Alignment raises the same-task rate from 3.8% to 34.2%, and its language similarity on tasks absent from the robot data (0.31) is close to that on shared tasks (0.32). sections.title: C Implementation Details
sections.content: Tokenizer. Table 7 lists the tokenizer settings of both experiments. Each observation is resized to 224 224 and encoded by frozen DINOv2-L, using features from its second-to-last layer. The visual encoder, transformer with 8 layers and 16 heads, maps the endpoint features of clip to 8 latent tokens. The quantizer is SoftVQ with 256 codes and softmax temperature of 0.25. The visual decoder, also with 8 layers, predicts the DINOv2 features of the future observation, and the action decoder predicts the action chunk from the quantized latents and the initial robot state with Huber loss (δ = 0.35). The visual reconstruction loss has weight 1, and the softmax temperature of Qi in equation (2.2) is 0.2. To provide robot clips as alignment targets for every human clip, each batch draws human and robot clips in equal numbers, and robot clips are gathered across GPUs. We optimize with AdamW (learning rate 104, β = (0.9, 0.95), weight decay 0.01) at constant learning rate, with gradient clipping at 1.0 and bf16 mixed precision. Table 7 Tokenizer settings. Horizon k: frame interval between the two endpoint observations of clip. In the real world, is 8 frames for one source of human videos, and 16, 8, or 4 frames for the other, chosen by motion speed so that slow motions span longer intervals. The VLM is Qwen3-VL-4B, and the action expert is separately parameterized Qwen3-style transformer with 0.6B parameters (36 layers, hidden size 768) that attends jointly with the VLM at every layer. The latent-action loss weight in equation (2.4) is λLA = 0.1. Pre-training starts from the Qwen3-VL-4BInstruct weights with randomly initialized action expert and 8 latent queries; mid-training starts from the pre-trained checkpoint, and post-training from the mid-trained one, keeping the same architecture throughout. Figure 11 Embodiments in RoboTwin 2.0. Frames of the same task performed by the target embodiment AlohaAgileX (left), whose complete trajectories form DR, and the non-target embodiment ARX-X5 (right), whose videos form DH . Atomic-Action Annotations on RoboTwin 2.0 RoboTwin 2.0 collects expert trajectories by running scripted program for each task with motion planner (Chen et al., 2025b). The program composes the task from manipulation primitives, and the planner executes each primitive as short sequence of arm motions and gripper commands. This execution divides each trajectory into atomic actions whose boundaries are given by the program. The program also specifies 22 the target object and the executing arm of each atomic action, so we describe each atomic action in language without manual annotation. These atomic actions typically last about one second. Figure 12 shows one episode divided in this way. We annotate the ARX-X5 and Aloha-AgileX trajectories with the same procedure. Figure 12 Atomic-action annotations on RoboTwin 2.0. Frames of one Aloha-AgileX episode of the beat block hammer task at the boundaries between consecutive steps of the task program. The description between two frames is the atomic action performed between them. Atomic-Action Annotations in the Real World Real-world trajectories are not generated by task program, so we annotate their atomic actions from the head-camera video with vision-language model (VLM), Doubao-Seed-2.0-Pro (Bytedance Seed, 2026). Each trajectory is first divided into subtasks, which come from existing subtask annotations where available and are otherwise proposed by the VLM from the video sampled at 1 Hz. The VLM then divides each subtask, sampled at 4 Hz, into the atomic actions of each hand. An atomic action is short, continuous interval with single manipulation intent, and its boundaries lie at observable changes, such as the start or end of motion or contact and separation between hand and an object. The VLM labels each atomic action with one of over dozen predefined common actions, or with label of its own when none of them applies, and describes it in one sentence that starts with The left hand or The right hand. Table 8 defines the 15 most frequent actions. Robot hands are referred to in the same way as human hands, so the descriptions do not depend on the embodiment. Figure 13 shows the distributions of the durations and labels of atomic actions. The peak at 4 comes from long hold intervals in human videos, which are annotated as consecutive 4 segments. Table 8 Definitions of the 15 most frequent atomic actions. Action Definition The hand stably holds an object, with the hand, fingers, wrist, and object all still. The fingers close to form stable grasp, including visible adjustments around it. The empty hand moves toward target and ends close to it before forming grasp. hold grasp reach transport The hand carries an object that has left its support to new location. The hand raises grasped object until it first fully leaves its support. lift The hand puts an object at target location, where it becomes stably supported. place The fingers open to end the grasp, and the hand separates from the object. release The hand pulls an object toward the body while keeping contact or grasp. pull The empty hand withdraws from the manipulation position. retreat The hand pushes on an object along the surface normal until it is visibly pressed in or triggered. press The hand moves with clear displacement that no more specific action describes. move The hand or held tool keeps contact with surface and moves along it to wipe it. wipe The hand aligns two objects and brings them into an inserted, nested, or fitted relation. mate The hand bends deformable object so that one part covers or lies against another. fold The hand pushes an aligned object through an opening until it is inside hole, slot, or container. insert 23 Figure 13 Statistics of real-world atomic-action annotations. (a) Distribution of atomic-action durations, with dashed lines marking the medians. (b) Frequency of the 15 most frequent predefined atomic actions, where others include composite labels and labels introduced by the VLM. Percentages are over the atomic actions of both hands. Real-World Platform All real-world experiments use Sharpa North robot1, wheeled full-body humanoid with two 7-DoF arms, each equipped with 22-DoF Sharpa Wave dexterous hand2. The Wave is human-scale, five-finger hand with vision-based tactile sensor in each fingertip; our policy does not use tactile inputs. The policy observes RGB images from head-mounted stereo camera and two wrist-mounted fisheye cameras, together with the joint angles of both arms, both hands, and five torso and neck joints. It predicts chunks of 32 joint-angle targets at 60 Hz, expressed relative to the current state and covering 63 actuated DoF, while images are captured at 30 Hz. Figure 14 shows the robot and its main components. (a) (c) (e) (b) (d) (f) Figure 14 Real-world platform. The Sharpa North robot comprises (a) head-mounted stereo camera, (b) two 7-DoF arms, (c) two 22-DoF Sharpa Wave dexterous hands, (d) two wrist-mounted fisheye cameras, (e) torso, and (f) wheeled base. 1https://www.sharpa.com/pages/north 2https://www.sharpa.com/pages/wave 24 Real-World Tasks For each task, we describe the goal and the success criterion. Figure 15 shows one teleoperated demonstration of each task. Gear assembly. The robot picks up three loose gears and assembles them onto the corresponding pegs of base plate. trial succeeds if all three gears are fully seated on the correct pegs with adjacent teeth engaged and remain in place after the robot releases them. Bimanual pouring. The robot transfers pills from source cup into receiving cup with both hands: one hand holds the receiving cup steady while the other lifts and tilts the source cup. trial succeeds if all pills are transferred into the receiving cup without visible spillage and both cups are placed upright on the table and released. Flower insertion. The robot grasps single flower by its stem, lifts it from holder, and inserts the stem into vase. trial succeeds if the stem is inside the vase and the flower remains supported by the upright vase after the robot releases it. Spoon scooping. The robot picks up spoon from its holder, scoops rice from bowl, and pours spoonful into target cup. trial succeeds if spoonful of rice is deposited into the target cup without visible spillage outside the containers and the spoon is returned to its holder and released. 25 Figure 15 Real-world tasks.
